walkthroughs.body_html:
Criminal Psychology — a core area of GCSE Psychology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Criminal Psychology brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Criminal Psychology.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Top-down offender profiling was developed by:
options: Canter
FBI
Lombroso
Eysenck

mcqs.q: Differential association theory was proposed by:
options: Sutherland
Eysenck
Bandura
Lombroso

mcqs.q: In Milgram's study, what percentage of participants gave the maximum 450V shock?
options: 35 percent.
100 percent (all of them).
65 percent.
All attachments are equally important.

mcqs.q: When is deception in research ever acceptable?
options: Always - psychologists can deceive freely.
When demand characteristics would otherwise invalidate the study, with thorough debrief and ethics approval.
Never - deception is always banned.
All attachments are equally important.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Bottom-up profiling”?
options: Lombroso's (1876) outdated theory that criminals are evolutionary throwbacks identifiable by physical features.
Sutherland (1939): criminal behaviour learned from associates whose pro-crime attitudes outweigh anti-crime ones.
Canter's UK approach: statistical analysis of crime scene data to derive profiles; investigative psychology.
Imprisonment aims to deter, rehabilitate, incapacitate and protect; UK recidivism around 48% within one year.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Eysenck's theory”?
options: Imprisonment aims to deter, rehabilitate, incapacitate and protect; UK recidivism around 48% within one year.
Criminals score high on extraversion, neuroticism and psychoticism (E, N, P); inherited nervous system underactivity.
Sutherland (1939): criminal behaviour learned from associates whose pro-crime attitudes outweigh anti-crime ones.
FBI approach (Ressler 1986): classify crime scene as organised or disorganised to infer offender characteristics.
